items.title: 'Dear Gen Z Conservationist': What India's Tiger Experts Wish Someone Had Told Them At 20
items.blurb: "The tiger is a large-hearted gentleman with boundless courage and that when he is exterminated — as exterminated he will be unless public opinion rallies to his support — India will be the poorer, having lost the finest of her fauna." — Jim Corbett Long before camera traps, GPS collars and scientific monitoring, Jim Corbett issued a warning that still rings true today: if India loses its tigers, it loses a part of itself. Every tiger roaming India's forests today is part of a conservation story that has taken decades to build. Over the last 50 years, the country has pulled the species back from the brink through Project Tiger, the Wildlife (Protection) Act, stronger laws, scientific monitoring and the dedication of thousands of forest guards, researchers and local communities. But today's challenge is very different. Saving tigers is no longer only about increasing their numbers. It is about protecting the forests they call home in a country where highways, railways, expanding towns and human aspirations increasingly overlap with wildlife habitats. This International Tiger Day, The Better India chose to move beyond census figures and policy reports to ask a more personal question: If India's leading tiger conservationists could write one letter to a young person dreaming of protecting wildlife, what would they say? Their answers draw on decades spent patrolling forests, working alongside local communities, combating poaching and shaping conservation efforts across the country. Together, they remind us that saving tigers has always been about protecting people, forests and the future they share. Dr Anish Andheria: 'Don't become an armchair conservationist' For Dr Anish Andheria, President and CEO of the Wildlife Conservation Trust (WCT), India's tiger story cannot be secured by awareness campaigns alone. Awareness, he says, only matters when it leads to action. Dr. Anish Andheria (extreme left) believes young people have a greater opportunity than ever to shape conservation conversations, but warns them against relying on shortcuts. Photograph: (Wildlife Conservation Trust) Speaking to The Better India , Andheria says that while conservation education has existed for years, the challenges in India's forests today demand a more informed and engaged generation. "Awareness by itself will not translate into anything unless it is put to use," he says. "Forests continue to be diverted in the name of development, defence and infrastructure. If there is hope, it lies with today's children." He believes young people have a greater opportunity than ever to shape conservation conversations, but warns them against relying on shortcuts. While social media has become an important tool for spreading awareness, he cautions against creating wildlife content without first understanding the science behind it. "Wildlife is not a subject where you can depend on AI or simply generate information," he says. More importantly, Andheria believes conservation cannot happen from behind a screen. "There is no point being an armchair conservationist," he says. "There is no shortcut to tiger conservation, or wildlife conservation for that matter." "Children should grow up confident enough to tell policymakers that our natural wealth cannot keep paying the price for everything else," Andheria says Photograph: (Anish Andheria) Instead, he encourages young people to step outdoors. Join nature clubs. Walk through neighbourhood forests, wetlands or beaches. Observe local biodiversity before dreaming of distant tiger reserves. Andheria is equally clear that wildlife tourism, when done responsibly, can become an important gateway into conservation, but only if people change the way they approach it. "I would always encourage children to visit national parks because tourism helps people connect with nature," he says. "But the narrative around tiger tourism has to change. People often think they're going only to see a tiger. Instead, they should learn about the entire ecosystem, the forests, the prey species, wildlife corridors, rivers and the communities living around these landscapes." For him, that broader understanding is essential because the biggest threats facing tigers today go well beyond the animal itself. "Young people entering conservation must understand issues like forest fragmentation, habitat degradation, poaching, illegal wildlife trade , and the impact these have on people living around forests," he says. "You cannot save tigers without protecting the landscapes they depend on." "Children should grow up confident enough to tell policymakers that our natural wealth cannot keep paying the price for everything else," he says. "Our water security, our economy and our future all depend on healthy ecosystems. Ecology and economy are deeply connected." His message to every young conservationist: "We have borrowed this planet from our children. When they, in turn, pass it on to the next generation, may they be proud to leave behind a world better than the one they inherited”. Jose Louies: 'Fight for conservation, not the glory of it' For Jose Louies, CEO of the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI), understanding India's conservation journey begins with understanding its history. Jose was also the Chief of Enforcement and lead the division that handled wildlife trade control and litigation. Despite India's remarkable recovery in tiger numbers, Louies believes that tiger poaching is far from over. Photograph: (Jose Louies, Facebook) "If I could return to 1947," he says, "I would want India to see tigers not as enemies of people but as part of our national heritage and people and there would be no reward for killing/hunting tigers ." Even after Independence, colonial attitudes towards wildlife continued to influence public thinking. Hunting remained socially celebrated, and policies often rewarded the killing of predators. Tigers were viewed as trophies or threats instead of an essential part of healthy ecosystems. Louies believes that mindset delayed India's conservation efforts before the country finally changed course. His own journey into tiger conservation began years later while travelling through tiger reserves with his mentor, the late Ashok Kumar. "There I learnt early that tiger poachers regularly infiltrate protected landscapes to kill the most enigmatic animals our forests hold," he recalls. "Tigers continue to be hunted for their body parts to supply domestic and international markets." Those experiences shaped the direction of his career. Despite India's remarkable recovery in tiger numbers, Louies believes one uncomfortable truth often goes unnoticed. "Tiger poaching is far from over," he tells The Better India. "While you are reading this piece, a tiger poacher is active somewhere in the country, stalking a tiger or perhaps having already made the kill." "Perhaps we were too focussed on increasing tiger numbers rather than improving quality of their habitats. This is something that future conservationists should work on to ensure that wildlife has a safe space in our country", Louise says. Photograph: (Steve Winter/National Geographic) For him, rising tiger numbers tell only one side of the story. The other unfolds far away from safari routes , where forest guards spend long days patrolling difficult terrain with limited resources, often risking their lives to protect wildlife. Looking ahead, Louies believes one of India's biggest priorities should be protecting the corridors that connect tiger reserves. These natural pathways allow tigers to move safely between forests, maintain healthy genetic diversity and reduce both conflict and poaching risks. His advice to young conservationists is simple but honest. "Fight for realistic conservation results, not the glory of conservation," he says. "This is not comfortable work. The rewards come through blood, sweat and hard work." And if a teenager wrote to him asking how they could help save tigers?: " There’s a lot of responsibility on your shoulders as there’s still a lot of work to be done. Educate yourself as much as you can about our wildlife and the conservation threats and successes that we have had. Whichever line of work you choose as your grow up, there’s always something you can contribute to ensure that India becomes a country where humans and wildlife coexist." Dr Rathin Barman: 'Know the animal before you try to save it' Some lessons stay with you forever. For Dr Rathin Barman, Director and Chief, Strategy and Liaison (North East), Wildlife Trust of India, one evening in Kaziranga National Park completely changed the way he looked at tigers. States that are home to tigers shoulder a national responsibility. They should therefore receive greater financial support from the Central Government to protect, restore, and manage tiger habitats effectively, Barman says. Photograph: (Wildlife Trust of India) An ageing rhinoceros had been killed. Deep inside the forest, a tiger was feeding on the carcass. "As dusk settled, I couldn't understand what I was seeing," he recalls. "The tiger was so deeply inside the rhino's body that it appeared to be some strange half-rhino, half-tiger creature." Then his eyes adjusted. "There he was," says Barman. "Completely absorbed in his meal. He had no idea we were only a few feet away." There was no panic. No urgency. "He ate with the confidence of a true king who knew he ruled the forest." The team quietly stepped back, leaving the tiger undisturbed. "That day my admiration became profound respect," he says. Years later, that moment continues to shape his approach to conservation. "Set enough land aside exclusively for tigers and its prey species. Don’t divert forest land for the activities which will affect the wild animals.", Barman says Photograph: (iStock) "The future of tigers is simple," he says. "Protect more forests. Set aside more land exclusively for wildlife." He believes India's conservation efforts must resist becoming driven by commercial interests. "Mass tourism and the relentless pursuit of tiger sightings must be regulated," he tells The Better india. "Wildlife conservation should never become merely a business." Instead, he calls for greater investment in tiger landscapes , stronger habitat protection and deeper involvement of communities living around forests. "We need to engage those who understand the culture and heartbeat of the locality." Barman also wants young conservationists to confront an uncomfortable chapter of India's past. "The so-called elite once killed tigers for fun," he says. "They proudly posed beside dead animals." Remembering that history, he believes, makes India's conservation success even more meaningful. But the challenges are far from over. "The reality is less glorious than what documentaries show," he says. "Tigers today are under pressure from unregulated tourism and relentless development. Forests are shrinking. Habitats are becoming fragmented." His advice to young conservationists is both practical and uncompromising. "Fight for the rights of free animals," he says. "Be prepared to face failures in the system. Stand against people who work only for personal wealth instead of ecological wealth." And before trying to save tigers? "Know the animal first," he says. "Understand its behaviour and ecological needs. Then make that curiosity infectious." Yash Magan Shethia: 'Every success carries a new responsibility' Yash Magan Shethia, Director, Wildlife Landscapes at WWF-India, writes his letter as though he is speaking directly to every young reader. He begins with a milestone. In 2010, at the Tiger Summit in St Petersburg, all 13 tiger-range countries committed to doubling the global wild tiger population by 2022. India achieved that goal, recording an estimated 3,682 wild tigers in its 2022 assessment. But, Shethia reminds us, the country's conservation journey began much earlier. One important lesson, Shethia says, came from the unsuccessful tiger reintroduction effort at Odisha's Satkosia Tiger Reserve in 2018. Photograph: (X/@Unitedfortigers) Around the time of Independence, naturalists estimated that India had nearly 40,000 tigers. As the newly independent nation focused on development, wildlife conservation received far less attention. Hunting continued, and organised shikar remained popular, he tells The Better India. Tiger numbers declined sharply. The turning point came with the Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972, followed by the launch of Project Tiger in 1973. In the years that followed, stronger institutions, better scientific monitoring and improved reserve management helped reverse the decline. Today, however, India's challenge has changed. Some reserves, including Tadoba and Pilibhit, support thriving tiger populations, while other suitable landscapes continue to have very few tigers. In 2010, at the Tiger Summit in St Petersburg, all 13 tiger-range countries committed to doubling the global wild tiger population by 2022. India achieved that goal, recording an estimated 3,682 wild tigers in its 2022 assessment Photograph: (BaghMitra) One important lesson, Shethia says, came from the unsuccessful tiger reintroduction effort at Odisha's Satkosia Tiger Reserve in 2018. "An ambitious programme to reintroduce tigers to the Satkosia Tiger Reserve in Odisha in 2018 ended when one of the two translocated animals died and the other had to be captured. This incident holds a key lesson, this being that the support of local communities is key to tiger recovery". India's long history of coexistence with wildlife, he believes, remains one of its greatest strengths. As tigers expand into new landscapes, local communities must become active partners in decisions around recovery, reintroduction and long-term management. His final message is hopeful. India's conservation journey has shown that the country is capable of learning from its mistakes, adapting its approach and improving over time. The next chapter, will depend on the same willingness to listen, learn and work together. Sandeep K Tiwari: 'Conservation cannot happen without people' For Sandeep K Tiwari, Chief of Conservation at the Wildlife Trust of India, one visit to the Sundarbans in 1996 changed the way he understood conservation. Until then, protecting wildlife had largely been an ecological challenge. But in the Sundarbans Tiger Reserve, he met families who had lost loved ones to tiger attacks. "That experience impressed upon me a fundamental truth," he says. "Conservation cannot succeed without addressing the socio-economic realities of local communities." Tiwari believes, protecting forests will always remain essential. But restoring the natural connections between them is equally important. Photograph: (X/@mesandeepTiwari) It was a lesson that has stayed with him ever since. Looking back, Tiwari believes one of India's biggest missed opportunities was failing to secure wildlife corridors before forests became increasingly fragmented. As roads, farms and settlements expanded, many protected areas became isolated ecological islands. Tigers dispersing between forests often had to move through villages and agricultural land, increasing conflict with people while leaving populations cut off from one another. For him, the future of tiger conservation lies beyond the boundaries of protected areas. Protecting forests will always remain essential. But restoring the natural connections between them is equally important. He also believes conservation has evolved in another important way. Earlier approaches often excluded Indigenous and forest-dependent communities from decision-making. Over time, that weakened trust. Today, community engagement, voluntary relocation where appropriate, compensation mechanisms and more inclusive conservation planning have begun to change that relationship. "That progress must continue," he says. As India continues to build roads, railways and other infrastructure, Tiwari believes conservation cannot remain an afterthought. Photograph: (Wikipedia/Davidvraju) Technology, too, has an increasingly important role to play. Better monitoring, ecological research, genetics and behavioural studies are helping conservationists make more informed decisions than ever before. But technology alone cannot save wildlife. "The people living alongside forests must be partners in conservation," he says. Community-led initiatives, including Primary Response Teams that help manage conflict and support the safe movement of wildlife, show what is possible when local people become part of the solution. As India continues to build roads, railways and other infrastructure, Tiwari believes conservation cannot remain an afterthought. Wildlife crossings, green infrastructure and connected landscapes will determine whether today's conservation successes endure. When a young person tells him, "I want to save tigers," his answer is immediate. "That's a fantastic idea." India needs researchers, policy advocates, communicators, scientists and conservation practitioners, he says. Because protecting tigers is about much more than one species. "It is about safeguarding the ecosystems that sustain biodiversity, ecological security and ultimately our own survival." More than letters, a shared message Each conservationist tells a different story. One learnt about the relentless threat of poaching. Another found lifelong respect for tigers while quietly watching one feed deep inside Kaziranga's forests. One reflected on India's conservation journey and the lessons it offers for the future. Another discovered, in the Sundarbans, that protecting wildlife is impossible without protecting people. Yet despite their different experiences, they all arrive at the same conclusion. Saving tigers has never been only about tigers. It is about protecting forests before they disappear. Keeping habitats connected. Working alongside communities instead of around them. Supporting the forest guards who patrol every day, often unseen. And recognising that every development decision leaves a lasting mark on wildlife. Perhaps that is India's greatest conservation lesson. As we approach #GlobalTigerDay , we celebrate India's remarkable tiger recovery, a conservation success over five decades in the making. From the launch of Project Tiger in 1973 to a network of 58 Tiger Reserves protecting 84,487 km² of forests, India's journey reflects the power… pic.twitter.com/XafZ6ppoJP — International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) (@IBCA_official) July 27, 2026 The country's tiger recovery was not the work of a single law, organisation or project. It was built over decades by thousands of people, forest guards, scientists, researchers, local communities, policymakers and conservationists — who refused to give up on a species that once seemed destined for decline. Now, a new generation inherits that responsibility. Whether they become biologists, engineers, teachers, filmmakers, lawyers or storytellers, each has a role to play in shaping the future of India's forests. As these four conservationists remind us, protecting tigers is not simply about ensuring one magnificent animal survives. It is about safeguarding the forests that clean our air, protect our rivers, support countless other species and ultimately sustain human life itself. The next chapter of India's tiger story has not yet been written. And perhaps it will be shaped by someone reading these words today.

items.title: The IFS Officer Who Raised a Tigress Like His Own Child
items.blurb: What happens when compassion becomes stronger than fear? 🐅❤️ In 1974, a frightened tigress cub was found alone on the banks of Odisha's Khairi River, too young to hunt and too weak to survive. She was brought to Saroj Raj Choudhury, the pioneering forest officer who helped shape Simlipal Tiger Reserve. Knowing she had little chance of surviving alone, he and his wife, Nihar Nalini Swain, brought the cub home, nursed her back to health, and named her Khairi. Khairi didn't grow up as a pet. She grew up as family. She drank milk from their hands, slept beside them, played freely, and formed an extraordinary bond with the couple who had saved her life. When Saroj later tried to return her to the wild, Khairi kept finding her way back home, the only place where she truly felt safe. Over the years, Saroj carefully observed her behaviour, contributing valuable insights to wildlife conservation and our understanding of big cats. In 1981, tragedy struck when Khairi died after contracting rabies following a dog bite. Her loss deeply affected Saroj, who passed away not long afterwards. Until her final days, Nihar continued to call Khairi her daughter. Their story reminds us that conservation isn't only about protecting wildlife, it's also about understanding, respect, and the profound connections that can exist between humans and the natural world. items.title: After Fire Destroyed His Orchard, This Jharkhand Farmer Grew a Rs 40 Lakh Cactus Farm
items.blurb: A hundred litchi trees, 300 mahogany trees, and 900 mango trees – this was the landscape across a 36-acre plot in Bichara village, Jharkhand, back in 2020. The land had been leased by 43-year-old farmer Chaitanya Kumar Ganjhu, who was determined to build something lasting. Every inch of the land was carefully revived to create a thriving orchard. But just three years later, even before the trees had matured, a fire reduced everything to ashes. To this day, Ganjhu does not know who set the blaze. Heartbroken, he could not even claim insurance because no police official was willing to register a complaint. "I didn't have insurance or any supporting document to establish my claim, and I returned home empty-handed," Ganjhu tells The Better India . The ideal species is Opuntia ficus-indica, often referred to as the spineless cactus, which thrives in Indian agroclimatic conditions, particularly in plateau areas such as Jharkhand. His farming journey had begun much earlier. In 2015, he had planned to start a lac farm, but limited resources forced him to change course. Instead, he began planting host trees, including 1,200 Indian jujube trees, only to lose them all in the devastating fire. Spineless cactus showed the way Looking back, Ganjhu now calls the fire a turning point. The tragedy left behind a vast stretch of empty land, forcing him to rethink what he could grow next. While exploring new opportunities in 2024, he learnt about central and state government efforts to promote cactus cultivation. Curious, he reached out to an engineer friend, who suggested that spineless cactus could be worth exploring. "I was excited because cactus farming was completely new to me. During my research, I discovered that natural leather can also be produced using Opuntia ficus-indica , a spineless cactus variety. Our native cactus has thorns, but this one doesn't," he says. Determined to learn more, Ganjhu spent weeks researching online before connecting with the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA). He saw cactus as more than an experimental crop. Unlike lac farming , which generates income only twice a year, cactus offered the possibility of a steadier source of earnings. Encouraged by the government's support for the crop, he contacted ICARDA's centre in Amlaha, Madhya Pradesh, to understand how to begin. Spineless cactus requires very little water, stays green even through harsh summers, and grows well in poor soils. What impressed him most was its resilience. Spineless cactus requires very little water, stays green even through harsh summers, and grows well in poor soils. Because it has no thorns, it can also be used as nutritious fodder for livestock. Confident that the crop had potential, Ganjhu purchased 10,000 cactus cladodes from ICARDA at Rs 10 each. In November 2024, he planted them across 2.5 acres of land at Gamhariya Jaltanda, becoming the first farmer in Jharkhand to cultivate spineless cactus on this scale. Today, his nursery has the capacity to produce nearly two lakh cactus plants every year. He currently grows 25 varieties. Among them, varieties such as Oretha de Elefante Africana, IPA-90-73, Copena V1, Mexica Folder-1278 and Additional-1258, sourced from Brazil, have performed particularly well. Each produces around 10 cladodes annually, compared to two or three from many of the other varieties. The slower-growing varieties, he says, are better suited for research than commercial cultivation. Water for irrigation comes from a solar-powered borewell. During summer, the plants are watered every five to six days because of the poor soil quality. In cooler months, watering once every 15 days is usually enough. Cow dung manure is applied twice a year. According to Dr Shiv Kumar Agrawal, Regional Coordinator for ICARDA's South Asia and China Regional Program and Head of the Food Legume Research Platform, grafting is unnecessary for spineless cactus because of the plant's natural ability to regenerate. "Grafting is not practised at ICARDA because, scientifically, Opuntia already has a high intrinsic regenerative capacity—its cladodes can readily form roots and new shoots without the need for a rootstock. Therefore, grafting does not provide a significant additional advantage in biomass production," explains Dr Agrawal. "Ganjhu is the only farmer to develop a cactus nursery in India. ICARDA introduced this technique and trained district-level officers and officials from the Watershed Development Department, but only Ganjhu took the initiative. Today, he is successfully growing healthy, disease-free spineless cactus in Jharkhand," says Dr Neha Tiwari, National Associate Scientist at ICARDA, Amlaha. Commercial opportunities in cactus farming What began as an experiment soon turned into a business opportunity. "The saplings are essentially cladodes," Ganjhu explains. "When I received an order for 30,000 saplings, I started pruning the mother plants, which made them shorter. I spoke to Dr Neha, who suggested growing them in polybags. From a single cladode, I was able to raise six to eight new saplings and fulfil the entire order." Each sapling takes about four months to grow in a polybag. To meet the demand, Ganjhu employed around 60 women from nearby villages to help prepare and nurture the saplings, creating an additional source of income for them. The economics, he says, are encouraging. A single cladode costs him about Rs 10. From that one cladode, he can grow six saplings, which together sell for around Rs 60. Even after accounting for labour, polybags, soil, irrigation and four months of care, he earns a profit of roughly Rs 25 from a single cladode. His first year was largely about recovering his investment. He spent around Rs 3 lakh procuring planting material and generated almost the same amount through sales. "It has reached the break-even point," he says. "Now the real profits will come." Last year alone, he sold around 30,000 cladodes and saplings at Rs 10 each, including transportation costs. Last year alone, he sold around 30,000 cladodes and saplings at Rs 10 each, including transportation costs. The cactus also serves another purpose on his farm. "I feed it to my goats. During summer, when grass becomes scarce, spineless cactus is a good source of nutrition because it contains high protein," he says. Now, he is waiting for the next big order. Betting on a growing sector Ganjhu believes the timing couldn't be better. The Government of India has identified spineless cactus cultivation as one of the focus areas under the Viksit Bharat framework. In Jharkhand, a project has been planned to cultivate nearly two lakh cactus plants across 400 hectares in different districts. For Ganjhu, this could create a significant opportunity. "If such projects need saplings, where will they source them from?" he asks with a smile. His goal is to become one of the state's key suppliers. Based on the number of cladodes currently available, he estimates he can produce close to four lakh saplings, creating a business worth nearly Rs 40 lakh while generating employment for many rural women. He also plans to participate in future tenders as cactus cultivation expands. Inspiring other farmers Ganjhu's success has already begun influencing neighbouring farmers. Last July, around 15 farmers from Raniyan village, nearly 40 km away in Khunti district, visited his farm after hearing about spineless cactus cultivation. They collected saplings and began planting them on their own land. These farmers are part of the state's cactus promotion initiative, launched in 2025, under which ICARDA has supported growers with free planting material, manure and assistance for land preparation. According to Ganjhu, nearly 40% of the participating farmers have successfully established their plantations. "The department is encouraging farmers to form a cactus growers' association," he says. "Even people who visit my farm often take home 10 or 12 saplings to plant. Slowly, people are beginning to see cactus differently." He enjoys introducing visitors to the wide range of cactus varieties growing on his farm. One of his favourites is Oretha de Elefante Africana, a slender variety that produces fewer cladodes but each weighing nearly half a kilogram. Another, popularly known as the Rabbit Cactus, gets its name from its distinctive pads that resemble rabbit ears. The familiar prickly pear variety also has commercial value. It is used in salads by restaurants and is cooked as a vegetable in several hilly regions. More than an ornamental plant Most people associate cactus with decorative pots or desert landscapes. But spineless cactus has far greater agricultural potential. Broadly, cacti are classified into ornamental, fruit-bearing and fodder varieties. Among these, spineless cactus has emerged as one of the most promising crops because it is easy to handle and serves multiple purposes. Researchers often describe it using the "5F" principle: food, fodder, fuel, fertiliser and fashion. Besides providing nutritious livestock feed, it can contribute to biogas production, organic fertiliser and even bio-leather, opening up new income opportunities for farmers. "The most suitable species is Opuntia ficus-indica , commonly known as nopal or spineless cactus," says Dr Neha Tiwari. "It adapts well to Indian agro-climatic conditions, including plateau regions like Jharkhand. It tolerates drought, fluctuating temperatures and poor soils, making it ideal for rain-fed and degraded lands." Chaitanya Ganjhu cultivates two lakh cactus plants on his 2.5-acre farm. Under field conditions, the plants can grow up to six or seven feet tall, depending on the variety and cultivation practices. Unlike seasonal crops, cactus does not have a fixed maturity period. However, farmers can begin harvesting cladodes around 10 to 12 months after planting, once the plant has established itself with four or five healthy cladodes. A crop built for the future For Ganjhu, spineless cactus is more than a profitable crop. He believes it could help farmers make better use of degraded land while opening up new income streams. "Our native cactus has no commercial value because of its thorns. But spineless cactus can change that," he says. "The soil conditions in Jharkhand are similar to those in parts of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal. If governments continue promoting it, many farmers could benefit." Experts agree. According to Dr Neha Tiwari, National Associate Scientist at ICARDA, Opuntia ficus-indica , commonly known as spineless cactus or nopal, is well suited to Jharkhand's climate because it can tolerate drought, poor soils and fluctuating temperatures. Beyond providing nutritious fodder, the crop has multiple uses. It can be processed into biogas, organic fertiliser and bio-leather, while also contributing to carbon sequestration. Since it requires relatively little water and maintenance once established, researchers see it as a promising option for climate-resilient farming. The initial investment is estimated at Rs 80,000 to Rs 1 lakh per hectare, excluding fencing. However, because the crop remains productive for 15 to 20 years, the long-term maintenance costs are relatively low. For Ganjhu, the bigger challenge is not cultivation but creating a market. "The biggest hurdle is finding buyers," he says. "At present, much of the produce is sent to a processing unit in Uttar Pradesh. If Jharkhand had its own processing unit, it would create jobs and increase farmers' incomes." Demand, however, appears to be growing. ICARDA has been working with the Jharkhand government to promote spineless cactus cultivation by supplying planting material and technical support. As more farmers take up the crop and government-led projects expand, Ganjhu hopes his nursery will become a key source of quality saplings across the state. From ridicule to recognition When Ganjhu first began planting Indian jujube trees years ago, many people in his village laughed at him. "They thought I was wasting my time because those trees already grew everywhere," he recalls. This time, when he introduced spineless cactus, there was scepticism again. But his family stood firmly beside him. Having seen his success in lac farming over the years, they trusted his instincts and encouraged him to continue experimenting. That confidence helped him build a better life. Income from lac farming enabled him to buy first a two-wheeler and later a four-wheeler. He also purchased land to build a house. In 2010, he received an award from the Jharkhand Chief Minister for his contribution to lac production. A farmer who kept looking ahead The fourth of six siblings, Ganjhu grew up in a lower-middle-class farming family. His late father cultivated paddy, oilseeds and vegetables using traditional methods. He attended State Samposhit High School, where three teachers taught nearly 1,000 students. "The teachers would write questions on the blackboard before moving to another classroom because there were so many students," he recalls. After completing school, he earned a BA (Honours) degree from Birsa College in 2003. Finding a job proved difficult. Instead, he discovered an opportunity in lac farming and has specialised in producing high-quality 'Bihan' lac since 2006. Today, he is married and has two sons. When he is not working on the farm, he enjoys travelling and watching cricket. Looking beyond his own farm Despite becoming India's first farmer to establish a commercial spineless cactus nursery, Ganjhu says he is only getting started. His long-term goal is to create a cooperative that can help farmers move beyond cultivation into processing and value addition. "Cactus can be used to produce biogas. The residue becomes fertiliser, and it can also be used to make bio-leather," he says. For him, the dream is no longer just about growing cactus. It is about creating an entire ecosystem around a crop that many once dismissed. After watching thousands of trees disappear in a single fire, Ganjhu could have walked away from farming altogether. Instead, he chose to begin again. Today, the same land that was once reduced to ashes is helping introduce a new crop to Jharkhand — one that could create livelihoods, strengthen climate-resilient farming and inspire more farmers to believe that sometimes, the boldest ideas are the ones worth planting.
